system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-10-06 20:12:00 to 2154-10-12 16:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for dizziness, worsening headache, and melena with a significant drop in hemoglobin from 37.5 to 25.5. Evaluation revealed guaiac-positive stool and a history of chronic GVHD, long-term steroid use, and anticoagulation with enoxaparin. CT head showed no acute intracranial process. EGD revealed duodenal erosions with recent bleeding, and colonoscopy showed a sigmoid ulcer and diverticulosis. Capsule endoscopy did not identify an active bleed. H. pylori infection was confirmed, and treatment with amoxicillin and clarithromycin was initiated. Enoxaparin was held during acute bleeding and restarted at a reduced dose of 40 mg daily prior to discharge. Hemoglobin improved to 10.5, and the patient was discharged home with plans for follow-up on pending biopsies, sirolimus level, and platelet function studies.
problems: Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage
Duodenal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction

Internal hemorrhoids without mention of complication
Diverticulosis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)
Herpes zoster without mention of complication
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Surgical operation with transplant of whole organ causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST RADIOGRAPH PERFORMED ON ___

COMPARISON:  Prior chest CT from ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Weakness, question pneumonia.

FINDINGS:  PA and lateral views of the chest are provided demonstrating
resolution  of bilateral subtle ground-glass and nodular opacities.  No large
effusion or pneumothorax is seen.  The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal.
Bony structures are intact.  Clips in the upper abdomen noted.

IMPRESSION:  Significant interval improvement in aeration of the lungs with no
residual consolidation seen.

HISTORY:  Patient with acute on chronic low back pain.

TECHNIQUE:  T1-T2 and inversion recovery sagittal and T2 axial images of the
lumbar spine.

COMPARISON:  Comparison was made with a prior abdominal CT of ___.

FINDINGS:

From T11 -12 to L5-S1 level, mild disk degenerative change and mild bulging
seen without spinal stenosis or foraminal narrowing.  No evidence of nerve
root displacement.

The superior endplate of L5 vertebra demonstrates mild compression with low T1
and slightly high convexity complex signal indicating of subacute to chronic
compression.  This finding was present on the previous abdominal CT.  There is
no acute compression fracture seen.

The distal spinal cord.  Paraspinal soft tissues are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:

Mild degenerative changes are seen in the lumbar region without spinal
stenosis or nerve root displacement.  Subacute to chronic compression of the
superior endplate of L5 vertebra identified as unchanged from previous
abdominal CT of ___.

TYPE OF THE EXAM:  CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

REASON FOR THE EXAM AND MEDICAL HISTORY:  History of CML presenting with
band-like pain, evaluate for fracture, pulmonary process suggestive of drug
toxicity.

TECHNIQUE:

Multiple axial CT images through the chest, abdomen and pelvis were obtained
post-administration of intravenous contrast and ingestion of oral contrast.

Coronal and sagittal reconstructions are obtained.

COMPARISON EXAMS:  ___ and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

FINDINGS:

CHEST:  Thyroid gland is normal in appearance.  There is no axillary,
supraclavicular, or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.  Heart is normal size.  There
is no pericardial effusion.  There are coronary artery calcifications and
calcified hilar lymph nodes probably likely secondary to prior granulomatous
disease.

Evaluation of the lung parenchyma demonstrates a right upper lobe granuloma as
well as residual patchy airspace ground-glass opacities which are less
extensive compared to the prior study.  There is no pleural effusion.

ABDOMEN:  Liver enhances homogeneously without evidence of focal masses. 
Patient is status post cholecystectomy.  Spleen is not enlarged.  Bilateral
adrenal glands and bilateral kidneys are unremarkable.  There is again seen a
cystic lesion within the pancreatic head, measuring 1.7 x 1.1 cm (2:60). 
There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation.  The remaining
pancreas is slightly atrophic, however, unremarkable.

There is no mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.  The oral contrast
has transited throughout the small loops of bowels, which are not dilated or
demonstrate any wall abnormality.

PELVIS:

Uterus is normal in appearance.  Urinary bladder is well distended without
evidence of focal masses.  There is gas distention of the sigmoid colon
without evidence of abnormal wall thickening or proximal obstruction.  There
is no lymphadenopathy or free fluid within the pelvis.

VASCULAR STRUCTURES:  There is no evidence to significant atherosclerotic
disease, aneurysmal dilatation.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  There is again seen a compression fracture of L5
vertebral body with endplate sclerosis, unchanged compared to the prior study.
T11 vertebral body, appears to have increasing sclerosis with relatively
stable loss of anterior body height. 

IMPRESSION:

1. Resolving bilateral patchy airspace opacities with residual scattered
minimal bilateral airspace opacity in the lungs.  No evidence of
lymphadenopathy within the chest, abdomen or pelvis.

2. Stable appearance of L5 compression fracture with increasing end plate
sclerosis of T11 and relatively stable loss of anterior verterbal body height,
indicating compression fracture. 

3. Stable size of pancreatic head cystic lesion, for which baseline MRCP is
recommended.

HISTORY:  ___ woman, with loss of height of T11; assess for acute
fracture.

COMPARISON:  CT chest, abdomen and pelvis on ___.  Also limited
comparison from MR lumbar spine on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar, multisequence T1- and T2-weighted images were
acquired through the thoracic spine, without IV contrast administration.

FINDINGS:  There is wedge deformity of the T11 vertebral body, with
approximately 25% of loss of height, anteriorly.  On the "water" IDEAL
sequence, there is diffuse but band-like hyperintensity involving
predominately the superior portion of the vertebral body.  The findings are
compatible with acute compression fracture. There is no evidence of extension
of bone edema to the posterior elements, and no retropulsion of its dorsal
cortex, canal compromise or effacement of the thecal sac.  The subjacent
portion of the spinal cord demonstrates no signal abnormality to suggest cord
contusion.  There is mild prevertebral fluid hyperintensity at T11. The dorsal
paraspinal soft tissues are unremarkable. 

There is no overall spinal malalignment. At T6-T7, a large (4.5 mm) right
paracentral disc protrusion indents the ventral spinal cord (6:8), and at
T7-T8, a left paracentral protrusion likely impinges upon the exiting left T7
nerve root (3:8, 6:13).  The remainder of the thoracic spinal canal remains
capacious.  Minimal degenerative changes are noted with minor endplate
irregularity at the T6-T7 and T12-L1 levels. 

The thoracic spinal cord remains normal in signal intensity and morphology.  

IMPRESSION:  
1.  Acute-to-subacute T11 anterior wedge compression fracture, without
retropulsion into the canal.  
2.  No evidence of spinal cord signal abnormality to suggest cord injury.  
3.  No thoracic spinal malalignment.
4.  T6-T7 and T7-8: Relatively large right and left paracentral disc
herniations, respectively, indent the spinal cord and impinge upon the exiting
nerve roots.

HISTORY:  New pancreatic mass.  Evaluate biliary tree.  

COMPARISON:  CT dated ___. 

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1 and T2 weighted images were acquired on a 1.5 Tesla
magnet obtained prior to, during and after the uneventful intravenous
administration of 7 mL of Gadavist.  The patient also received 2.5 mL of
Gadavist diluted with 75 mL of water p.o..  

A non-breath hold protocol had to be performed as the patient could not hold
her breath.  

FINDINGS:

There are multiple cystic lesions within the pancreas, with the largest
measuring 1.8 cm within the head of the pancreas (6:1).  There is no definite
communication between the cystic lesions and the main pancreatic duct.  The
main pancreatic duct is of normal caliber.  The pancreas is otherwise atrophic
and there is lipomatous replacement of pancreatic parenchyma. 

The biliary tree is normal.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy.  No
filling defects in the biliary tree. 

The liver is within normal limits.  No focal liver lesions.  The portal and
hepatic veins are patent.  Note is made of a surgical clip adjacent to the
posterior aspect of the right lobe of the liver (16:13). 

The kidneys and adrenals are within normal limits.  The spleen is
unremarkable.  The visualized small and large bowel is unremarkable.  No
retroperitoneal or mesenteric adenopathy.  The lung bases are clear. 

There is an anterior wedge compression fracture at T11 with bone marrow edema
identified within this vertebral body, consistent with an acute/subacute
fracture.  There is also a chronic anterior wedge compression fracture of L5. 
There is approximately 25% loss of vertebral body height at both levels.  No
destructive osseous lesions.  

 IMPRESSION:

1.  Multiple cystic lesions in the pancreas, largest measuring 1.8 cm in the
head of the pancreas.  Statistically these most likely represent side branch
IPMNs.  Follow-up MRI in 6 months is recommended. 

2. Normal biliary tree. 

3.  Anterior wedge compression fractures at T11 and L5 with <25% loss of
vertebral body height. Edema at fracture site at T11 suggestive of
acute/subacute fracture. L5 compression fracture appears chronic.

HISTORY:  Increased abdominal pain, evaluate for abdominal pathology.

COMPARISON:  CT torso from ___, MRCP from ___ and abdominal
radiograph from ___.

FINDINGS:

Two frontal images of the abdomen demonstrate a nonspecific bowel gas pattern.
There are a few air-fluid levels in the right lower quadrant; however, air is
seen within the colon to the rectum.  No dilated loops of small bowel are
appreciated.  No free intraperitoneal air is identified.

IMPRESSION:

Nonspecific bowel gas pattern with no free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having back pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been going on for years, but it got much worse two weeks ago when I stood up from sitting. It’s sharp and goes into my abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Does it get worse with movement? Any numbness or weakness in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s worse when I bend down. But no, I don’t have any weakness. I can walk fine. I’ve also been feeling dizzy when I stand up quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. We’ll check your blood pressure and do some imaging. Given your history, we need to be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many issues since my transplant. I just want to know what’s causing this new pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start with a CT scan of your chest, abdomen, and pelvis to look for fractures or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT showed your old L5 fracture is stable, but there’s new concern about T11. We’re ordering an MRI of your thoracic spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: T11? Is that a new fracture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a new compression fracture at T11. The MRI will confirm if it’s recent and whether there’s any nerve involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that why the pain is so bad now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s very likely. The good news is there’s no spinal cord compression. You’re not at risk for paralysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll consult spine surgery. You may need a brace. We’ll also adjust your pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI confirmed an acute-to-subacute compression fracture at T11. No nerve damage. Spine team recommends a brace and conservative management for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. They’ll see you as an outpatient to discuss vertebroplasty if the pain doesn’t improve with meds and the brace.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My abdomen has been sore too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. Your liver enzymes are a bit high, which could be from your GVHD or meds. We’ll do an MRCP to check your pancreas and bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRCP is back. You have several small cysts in your pancreas, the largest is 1.8 cm. They’re likely benign, called IPMNs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cysts? Are they dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are harmless, but they need monitoring. We recommend a repeat MRI in six months to make sure they’re not growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. And my abdominal pain—could that be from the cysts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The cysts aren’t pressing on anything. Your pain may be from muscle strain or your chronic GVHD. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on a back brace and added morphine twice daily for the fracture pain. How’s it feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but I’m a bit groggy. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, morphine can cause drowsiness at first. We’ll adjust the dose if needed. Keep taking your oxycodone as needed too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood counts are stable. White count is low, but that’s expected with your history. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’re adding docusate and senna to help. Drink plenty of fluids and try to move around a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been having trouble sleeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can continue your lorazepam as needed. Try to keep a regular schedule and avoid screens before bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your liver enzymes are stable. Blood sugar is a bit high, but we’re managing it with your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know steroids make my diabetes worse. Can we lower my prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You still need it for your GVHD. We’ll work with your specialist to taper it slowly when safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. What about my blood thinner? I’ve had bleeds before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a low dose of enoxaparin, 40 mg daily. Your hemoglobin hasn’t dropped, so it’s safe to continue for your clotting risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The spine team reviewed your case. They recommend continuing the brace and pain control. Follow up in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment. I’m glad I’m not a candidate for surgery yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray was nonspecific—no blockage. Pain seems musculoskeletal. Keep using the lidocaine patch and flexeril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The patch helps. My dizziness has improved too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s likely positional and related to your blood pressure or meds. Keep rising slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wear the brace as instructed, take your pain meds on schedule, and avoid heavy lifting. Follow up with spine clinic and repeat MRI in six months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual medications—sirolimus, prednisone, insulin, and enoxaparin. We added metoclopramide for stomach discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep track. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if pain worsens or you have fever, weakness, or new symptoms. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—the pancreatic cysts aren’t cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, they’re not cancerous. But we monitor them because rare types can change over time. The six-month MRI will help us track that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will review your meds and brace use. Discharge paperwork is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve scheduled my follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re doing well. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your bruising is from the blood thinner and low platelets. Avoid falls and report any large bruises or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed that. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your oxygen levels are good, and you walked to the bathroom fine. You’re ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thanks to the whole team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call with any concerns. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a great day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe home. Remember: brace, meds, and follow-ups. You’re doing great.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with acute-on-chronic low back pain radiating to the abdomen, two weeks after a sudden onset. Imaging revealed a new acute-to-subacute compression fracture at T11, with a stable chronic L5 fracture. She was managed conservatively with a back brace, morphine, oxycodone, and muscle relaxants, with spine surgery follow-up planned for possible vertebroplasty if needed. An MRCP showed multiple pancreatic cysts, likely side-branch IPMNs, with a recommendation for repeat MRI in six months. Her chronic conditions—GVHD, diabetes, osteoporosis, and history of DVT/PE—were maintained on current therapies, including enoxaparin, prednisone, sirolimus, and insulin. She remained stable, pain-controlled, and neurologically intact, and was discharged home with follow-up plans for spine and imaging.
